title: Letter-for-Letter Cipher
statement:
You get two strings s and t of the same length. Decide whether t could be an encoding of s by a simple substitution cipher.

The cipher replaces every occurrence of a character with one fixed character, at every position. A character may be replaced by itself. Two different characters can never be replaced by the same character.

Return true if such a cipher exists, otherwise false.

examples.why: n → d and o → e turn "noon" into "deed".
The e at index 1 would become a, but the e at index 3 would become m. One character cannot have two codes.
Each letter of s gets one code, but e and a would both become o. Checking only the s → t direction misses this.

constraints: s and t contain printable ASCII characters
hints: Read both strings side by side. Each pair of characters at the same index is a claim: "this character encodes to that one".
Store the claims in a map from s-characters to t-characters and reject any contradiction. Is that enough? Try s = "ab", t = "zz".
Keep a second map from t-characters back to s-characters (or a set of codes already used). Both directions must stay consistent.

explain.intuition:
A substitution cipher is a one-to-one mapping. "One" on the left side: each character of s always becomes the same character. "One" on the right side: no two characters of s share a code. A single map from s to t only checks the first rule. That is why "team" vs "look" slips through it: e and a each map consistently, but both to o.

So scan once with two maps, one per direction, and stop at the first contradiction. Another way to see it: both strings must have the same shape, meaning that the character at each position first appeared at the same index in both strings.
steps: Create two empty maps: fwd (s-char → t-char) and back (t-char → s-char).
For each index i, let a = s[i], b = t[i].
If fwd has a with a value other than b, or back has b with a value other than a, return false.
pitfalls: Checking only one direction. "ab" vs "zz" must be false.
Comparing sorted character counts. "abab" and "ccdd" have the same counts but different shapes.
Assuming only lowercase letters and using a 26-slot array. Spaces, digits and symbols are allowed here.

complexity.space: O(k), k = number of distinct characters

solutions.title: Compare every pair of positions
solutions.idea: The strings match exactly when, for every pair of positions, s has equal characters there if and only if t does.

solutions.title: Two maps, one per direction
solutions.idea: Record the code for each s-character and the source of each t-character. Any contradiction in either map means no cipher exists.

solutions.title: Compare first-seen indexes
solutions.idea: Replace each character by the index where it first appeared. Two strings fit one cipher exactly when these index sequences are equal.

followups: Group a list of words into buckets of words that share a shape. What key do you use for the map?
Match a pattern like "abba" against a sentence of words ("red blue blue red"). What changes?
